references.text: Miriam repeats the same refrain verse that Moses sings, confirming the victory over the Egyptians at the Sea of Reeds.
The psalm refers to how the people of Israel believed in the Lord's word and sang his praise after crossing the Sea of Reeds.
The same formula of praise is used: The Lord is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation.
Isaiah quotes from Moses' song and uses the expression about the Lord as strength and song.
Revelation describes the holy ones singing 'the song of Moses, God's servant,' and 'the song of the Lamb' as an eschatological parallel to the victory song at the Sea of Reeds.
Moses' farewell song in Deuteronomy begins similarly with a call to listen to the song that praises the Lord.
Deborah and Barak sing a victory song to the Lord after defeating Sisera, following the same pattern as Moses' victory song.
The psalm praises the Lord who shook Pharaoh and his army in the Sea of Reeds, recalling the same event.
Narrative explanation of the poetic proclamation in 15:1 regarding the miracle at the Red Sea.
Theological contrast: From a hymn of praise over Egypt's fall (Ex 15) to a lament over that same nation's downfall (Ezekiel).
Direct allusion: The heavenly song fulfills and confirms Moses' song about God's victory.
Thematic parallel: Creation's song of praise as a response to the Lord's historical deliverance of Jacob/Israel.
Confirmation that the song in Ex 15 was written down and handed down as a central part of the tradition of faith.
